extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations; PR managers and organizational leaders
extracted.subtask_description: Principles, organizational roles, ethical limits, and historical tactics of public relations—guidance for how PR should be organized and practiced in organizations and campaigns. Includes strategic, managerial, tactical, and ethical criteria illustrated with historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into management (dominant coalition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Public relations has become an integral part of most organizations’ management structure—the dominant coalition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top management increasingly recognizes PR as essential; high-level practitioners with manager-role knowledge join or are consulted by executive decision-making groups (see Chapter 2 on roles). PR gains impact when it participates in major decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioners as counselors and strategic planners
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners in public relations firms increasingly serve as counselors and strategic planners, rather than mere press agents and communication technicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize advisory, strategic functions over tactical-only work; develop capabilities to provide counsel and planning to organizational leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trend to small expert departments and outsourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prediction that traditional, large, central PR departments will become relics; very tight, small and expert departments are likely to become the norm and outsourcing may be the word most commonly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR chiefs may use a broad array of consulting firms, including small local firms; agencies must demonstrate comparative advantage versus small local rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain core PR responsibilities in-house
rubrics_metrics.description: A firm may be a counselor, but not a substitute or surrogate for handling the vital PR roles; rather than build huge staffs outsourcing can be cost-effective for noncritical functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outsource noncritical tasks but keep high-priority, core responsibilities internal to preserve control over vital PR roles and organizational voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate communications specialists from other professional firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Management consulting firms have added 'communications specialists' to their staffs; some large law firms also offer 'public relations counsel' to complement legal counsel in high-profile cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect cross-professional entrants; coordinate communications counsel with legal and management advisors to provide integrated services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote candor and socially responsible actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations has an impact when people begin to tell each other that candor in communication is the best policy and that socially responsible actions are in the best interest of the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate organizational norms of candor and social responsibility to strengthen PR effectiveness and internal confidence in staff and counselors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit disclosure when appropriate (competitive, security, ethical, legal constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposing a clean organization to public gaze ... does not mean that everything about the organization should be made public. In business, there are competitors to consider. In the military, there are security considerations. In health institutions, there are ethical limitations on disclosure of patient information. In government agencies, there are political and regulatory factors. Everywhere there are legal pros and cons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance transparency with legitimate restrictions; use specialized staff or counsel to determine what to disclose and what to withhold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of an organization to implement PR actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of an organization to implement actions made possible by a public relations campaign: the Sons of Liberty ... and the Committees of Correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful campaigns require an organizational structure to coordinate, sustain, and implement tactics and follow-through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use identifiable, emotion-arousing symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of symbols that are easily identifiable and arouse emotion: the Liberty Tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select symbols that condense and evoke feeling; symbols help brand and anchor campaign messages in public memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use slogans to compress complex issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of slogans that compress complex issues into easy-to-quote, easy-to-remember stereotypes: 'Taxation without representation is tyranny.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft succinct, memorable lines that frame complex arguments simply for broad public uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ staged events to catch attention and crystallize opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Staged events that catch public attention, provoke discussion, and thus crystallize unstructured public opinion: the Boston Tea Party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design events to generate news, provoke conversation, and create focal points around which public opinion can coalesce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get your interpretation out first
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of getting your side of a story to the public first, so that your interpretation of events becomes the accepted one: the Boston Massacre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize speed and framing to establish the dominant narrative before opponents or alternative interpretations take hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained saturation campaigns across channels
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity for a sustained saturation campaign using these techniques through all available channels of communication to penetrate the public mind with a new idea or a new conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated messaging across multiple media and channels to achieve penetration and long-term attitude or behavior change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create events when none exist to serve campaign needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Adams would create events to meet a need if none were at hand to serve his purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If natural events do not support your objectives, plan and stage events that will create news opportunities and frame issues favorably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agentry techniques can build attention but risk credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Press agentry—systematic efforts to attract or divert public attention—was used to promote land settlement and build box office personalities; as press agents grew in number and exploits became more outrageous ... they would arouse the hostility and suspicion of editors, and inevitable that the practice and its practitioners would become tainted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that sensationalism can gain attention but may damage long-term credibility and relationships with media gatekeepers; weigh short-term visibility against reputational risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance and merit underlie effective public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: When Westinghouse’s AC system won public acceptance despite the Edison–Insull propaganda scare campaign, it demonstrated 'that performance and merit are the foundation stones of effective public relations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained public acceptance depends ultimately on the actual quality and performance of the product, service, or policy being promoted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of white papers/controlled publications to sway informed audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical analogies: Swaying Early Adopters (Committees of Correspondence), The White Paper (Thomas Paine’s Common Sense), Product Launch Press Release (Declaration of Independence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy long-form persuasive documents (white papers, pamphlets) and formal announcements to influence opinion leaders and early adopters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from one-way persuasion to two-way reciprocal communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions evolved to include two-way communication and relationships; Webster’s: 'The art or science of developing reciprocal understanding and goodwill.' British Institute: build 'mutual understanding between an organization and its publics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor interactive, dialogic approaches that incorporate feedback and relationship-building rather than solely one-way propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile organizational behavior with the public interest (Childs’ view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harwood L. Childs: the basic function 'is to reconcile or adjust in the public interest those aspects of our personal and corporate behavior which have a social significance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame PR as aligning organizational actions with social expectations and public interest; use PR to mediate social impacts and adjust behaviors accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic use of media influence (paid/parked content, advertising)
rubrics_metrics.description: Banks were the first businesses to use the press for this purpose; by loans to editors and placement of advertisements, they influenced many newspapers and silenced others. In March 1831 ... authorized ... to saturate the nation’s press with press releases, reports, and pamphlets pushing the bank’s case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine earned, paid, and owned media strategically to shape coverage; be mindful of ethical implications and potential backlash when attempting to manipulate media channels.
